hints.hint: In "I don't know" puzzles, ignorance is a fact about the speaker's own value, never about how many pairs the public data allows. Note anything the problem leaves unsettled, such as which of two quantities was published; the speakers do not know it either. For a holder of v, list one partner per option (public minus v, public over v), keeping only those obeying the domain rules; equal values are allowed. If one option alone would pin the partner, that is no contradiction and eliminates no option: ignorance just needs two or more legal partners across options. Record that as a condition P on the first speaker's value. Then use it: every partner the second speaker lists is the first speaker's value, so discard partners failing P and require two or more still left. Answer with a value passing that stronger test; never tie-break by primality, size, or looks.
hints.subagent_summary: My 8 rollouts scored 1/8 (exec 149.318): 3 hit the 16384-token cap, 4 boxed a wrong divisor (143 x3, 13 once justified explicitly by primality). Every failure judged ignorance by counting pairs consistent with 2002 itself rather than by what the holder of v can still not distinguish; several wrote 'she knows the other is public minus v, so she knows', called that reading impossible (impossible appears 17-54 times in the loopers), then collapsed to one reading and picked a factor on looks. Not one rollout carried the first announcement forward as a condition and applied it to the second speaker's candidate partners. The incumbent already says 'predicate' abstractly and the model even echoes the word without doing it, so the revision leads with the misconception itself (ignorance is about your own value, not the public count) and states the carry-forward concretely: the second speaker's partners ARE the first speaker's value, so they must satisfy P and two must remain.

hints.hint: To find where ALL solutions lie, derive one necessary condition, never the solutions. From (z-a)^n = c(z-b)^n take moduli of whole sides: |z-a|^n = |c||z-b|^n. Only then nth-root that scalar: |z-a| = k|z-b|, k^n = |c|; write |c| as a prime power and divide its exponent by n. Square to clear moduli (z = x+iy); a zero x^2+y^2 coefficient means a line, else divide by it and complete the square for center and r > 0. Containment was all that was asked: never enumerate roots. Audit with two points instead: the locus meets line ab where z-a = +-k(z-b); these end a diameter, so their midpoint is the center, half their gap is r. A mismatch indicts k, not the method.
hints.subagent_summary: All 8 rollouts correct (3.8k-6.6k tokens, 4-25 hedges), so training is saturated and the lever is transfer and wasted budget. Every rollout had the right circle inside its first ~600 tokens, then spent most of the rest enumerating the n solutions (11-44 exponential/root-of-unity expressions each) despite the incumbent's flat ban. The worst (6.6k tokens, 25 hedges) rewrote to ratio form, mis-solved a branch, got a point failing its own modulus condition, and burned ~4k tokens escaping that self-inflicted contradiction. Two others closed by calling the condition 'necessary and sufficient': right answer, wrong logic that will not transfer. Diagnosis: a prohibition with no substitute leaves the verification urge nowhere to go. So the revision keeps modulus-first plus the exponent-arithmetic k rule and swaps the bare stop rule for a bounded portable audit: the two collinear locus points end a diameter, a two-point check on center and radius that also catches a wrong k.

hints.hint: Union = summed areas minus overlap, so minimize overlap. Frame it on the covering shape's own edges: from the shared point take the two edge directions leaving it as axes, so the cover is the wedge x >= 0, y >= 0. A corner spans only the plus side of both directions, so never extend that shape a full side both ways from the point and never treat the point as its center. Sign-test each vertex of the other shape S: covered iff both coordinates are >= 0. One negative coordinate kills containment; the point lying inside S kills disjointness. Overlap is S clipped to the wedge; compute that one area in the easiest orientation and record the union. If rotating the wedge by its own angle carries each clipped piece to the next, the pieces are congruent, overlap is constant in the angle, and your union is already optimal: state it and stop. No second orientation, no tangency.
hints.subagent_summary: 6/8 correct. Both failures hit the 16384 cap, neither committing a wrong answer. Failure A never built the corner frame: it put the big square's corner at the shared point but extended it a full side BOTH ways on each axis (-1.5..2.5), so that point became interior, the small square looked wholly covered (overlap 1), and it then spent 70 'tangent' mentions before guessing 4.5. Failure B did use the quadrant frame, computed the correct aligned overlap by ~4.5k chars and stated the union, then reopened 'maybe rotating shrinks it' and burned ~55k chars building rotated-square inequalities and vertices without closing. Winners reached that same first value and closed fast. So this revision makes the frame constructive (edge directions from the shared point; the cover is the plus-side wedge, so a corner cannot surround the point), makes the bound executable via per-vertex sign tests, and hard-bans a second orientation.

hints.hint: A maximum count is an upper bound meeting a matching construction; produce both. Write the target at index n as its own formula T(n), degree 1 for an arithmetic progression. Never label a function by the term index and never subtract adjacent terms: neighbours may use different functions, so no equation follows. A function is constrained only at the indices where it was used and free elsewhere, so nothing forces its consecutive values to step by the common difference. Bound by pigeonhole: with k indices and N functions, some P serves at least k/N of them, each a root of P - T, not identically zero since T cannot cancel P's degree-d leading term; so k/N <= d, k <= N x d. Tightness: give each function a block n_1..n_d and set P = T + c(x-n_1)...(x-n_d), c nonzero: full degree, equal to T there.
hints.subagent_summary: 5/8 with the incumbent. All 3 failures shared one setup error: they labelled a polynomial per term (P_i at index i), imposed P_{i+1}(x+1)-P_i(x)=d, found it non-constant, and concluded one term per function. Two stopped there, answering N=10 and even 1; the N=10 one had already read the N x d cap and explicitly overrode it as inapplicable. The third truncated while chaining adjacent terms into a per-term construction, never grouping indices by function. So the per-group cap keeps losing to the belief that reuse would force one function's own consecutive values to step by d, and stating Bound = N x d as a rule invites override. This revision derives the product instead of asserting it: pigeonhole forces some function to serve k/N indices, whose root count caps k. It also adds that a function is constrained only at its own indices and free elsewhere, which is exactly what kills the reuse objection.

hints.hint: Base 1/k: height y means argument k^-y, so negative y means a LARGE argument. Fit parameters from the given points. A vector equality is ONE constraint: read the displacement (dx,dy) off it, not via midpoints. Carry one unknown, a vertex at (t, f(t)), closure f(t+dx)=f(t)+dy. Gap dy becomes one factor k^-dy on the argument, a rational equation in t. A given vertex's x MUST solve it, as the coincident vertex fits everything; if not, your factor is inverted. If so, divide it out; the rest is linear. Never read a new height as a fresh log; ANCHOR it: write its argument as a given vertex's argument times a power of the base as written, then offset that vertex's known height by that exponent. Anchor both heights so; they must differ by dy. Area = |cross product| of edges.
hints.subagent_summary: 7/8 correct (149.322); every rollout finished, none hit the cap, so the pipeline is sound and exactly one step leaks. The failure fit a=1,b=-1, took the displacement correctly, formed the closure, got the right quadratic, and correctly rejected the degenerate root reproducing a given vertex. It then evaluated the surviving vertex's height as a fresh log of an argument below 1 and copied the reciprocal exponent, getting a negative height where the true one is positive; the partner height inherited the flip, both new points left the curve, and the cross product came out about a third of the true area. The incumbent only fixes the forward height-to-argument direction, which that rollout used flawlessly. So the revision removes the reverse log evaluation entirely: express the new argument as a given vertex's argument times a power of the base as written and offset that vertex's known height, cross-checked from both given vertices, which flags any sign flip immediately.

hints.hint:
Never model the final pile as a uniformly random permutation. Only stack-realisable orders occur, Catalan-many, far below n!, so most permutations have probability 0 and reachable ones carry unequal weights; 1/n, 1/n! and favourable-over-total are all wrong.

Pin orientation from the last move, not intuition: the final carry lays an item on TOP, so a pile's bottom is its FIRST arrival. Restate each named position as an arrival rank; writing bottom = carried last means you flipped the pile.

Then turn the event into a constraint on the order of carries, write that order out step by step, and label each step: one legal carry, weight 1; two legal carries with the event picking one, weight 1/2. Freeing a buried item early forces one choice per item above it, so expect several halves, not one. Multiply along the order, then sum the orders satisfying the event.
hints.subagent_summary: 1/8 this round (idx 0, and even it reached the value after writing bottom = carried last). Six of eight (idx 1,2,3,4,5,6) explicitly declared the destination bottom to be the item carried LAST, inverting the pile, then read the answer off a uniform model: 1/4 from 'each bag equally likely to be last' (idx 1,3,5,6) or a bare 1/2 (idx 2,4); idx 3,6 also gave 1/24 for the earlier part. Idx 7 used favourable-over-total, 1 of 2^4, giving 1/16. So the incumbent's declarative arrival-rank rule and its verbal ban on 1/n both fail: the flip survives and uniformity is re-imported for the graded part. This revision derives orientation from the last carry instead of asserting it, and replaces the ban with a reason uniformity is impossible: reachable orders are Catalan-many, not n!, and unequally weighted. Forced/free 1/2 pricing and the run-of-halves warning are kept.

hints.hint:
Large stated size, one entry asked: never do algebra at that size, never carry it as a symbol. Read the law off small cases in exact numbers.
Scale the toy by unknown count: n unknowns get exactly n conditions TOTAL, exponents 1..n -- so n-1 zero conditions plus the nonzero one last. n zero conditions plus a nonzero one is n+1 conditions for n unknowns; that over-determined toy forces every unknown to 0 and looks contradictory. Then drop one zero condition; never call a toy unsolvable or rescale again.
Solve n=2,3,4 by elimination in exact fractions, checking each answer in its own conditions.
Take growth and sign from ratios of consecutive answers: factorial, binomial, power. Computed numbers outrank any formula. Expanding a large product of linear factors for one coefficient never terminates; if you drift there, return to numbers. Substitute the stated size once and stop.
hints.subagent_summary: 0/8 this round (same hint scored 5/8 in r14), so the ladder is fragile and the failure is concentrated in one place: building the toy. Every rollout tried small cases, but 7 of 8 wrote n zero conditions PLUS the nonzero one, i.e. n+1 conditions for n unknowns. That toy forces all unknowns to 0, so rollouts read it as a contradiction or as the method failing, spent 1000-3000 tokens re-arguing the scaling, then abandoned numbers for symbolic work at the stated size (products of linear factors, harmonic sums); 6 hit the 16384 cap. The two that terminated reported laws fit from corrupted toys. The incumbent says 'n conditions' but never says the zero conditions therefore number n-1, so the miscount is not detectable from it. This revision states the total-count rule, names the all-zeros symptom, and gives the one-line repair instead of only forbidding renegotiation.

hints.hint: Let N be the unstated count of identical units; recover it from integrality, not from the story. If every per-unit share must be whole, N divides each listed total, so admissible N are their common divisors. Select deliberately: if the text bounds the count (a range, at least, at most), keep only divisors inside that window; otherwise take the maximum feasible count, their gcd. When the story counts groups (streets, rows, batches), write N = groups x units-per-group and solve for the second factor; a group count is never N by itself. Fix each figure's role from its own label: one headed as an aggregate stays aggregate, one labelled per unit stays per unit. If a step stalls, recheck arithmetic; never reassign a role or shrink N to escape. Then sum all components, divide by N, apply any markup or discount as one factor, and answer the question asked.
hints.subagent_summary: 7/8 public rollouts correct (train_i 0.875, receipt 149.325). The single failure was not arithmetic: it derived gcd 15, listed admissible counts, and had both candidate per-unit splits verified, then reopened the aggregate-vs-per-unit reading of the listed figures, re-read village totals as per-house amounts, produced an absurd count, declared a contradiction, and looped that same paragraph four times (15.5k tokens, 40 backtracks) before abandoning the maximum and lifting the story's group count as N. Correct rollouts showed the same churn more weakly (10-48 backtracks). So the incumbent's promise to 'decide once ... then stop revisiting' is not actionable, because nothing tells the student how to decide or what to do when stuck. I replaced it with a rule that fixes each figure's role from its own label and forbids reassigning a role or shrinking N to escape a stuck step, keeping every proven mechanism intact.

hints.hint: If same-degree unknown maps satisfy p(q(x))=q(p(x)), skip the degree-n^2 coefficient system. Seek a common fixed point r and center: p(x)=r+A(x-r)^n, q(x)=r+B(x-r)^n, so composing only multiplies constants, forcing AB^n=BA^n. Cancel only the common factor AB, leaving A^(n-1)=B^(n-1); cancelling a higher power deletes the branch you need, stranding you at the false p=q. Inside the ansatz the identity then holds automatically - expect that, not underdetermination; match free parameters to independent givens. Solve those by symmetric combination, never by ratio - dividing conditions multiplies exponents into a high-degree equation whose roots you can only guess at. Add the two to cancel the sign-flipped part and pin the center; subtract to pin the scale. Then evaluate the asked inputs centered.
hints.subagent_summary: All 8 rollouts correct (~4.1-9.1k tokens), so training is saturated and the loss is transfer. Two recurring detours dominate the wasted tokens. (1) Mis-cancellation: several rollouts reduce AB^n=BA^n by dividing out AB^2 (or B^3=A^3), collapse to A=B, then spend long passages declaring the ansatz contradictory before recovering the sign-flipped branch. (2) The 9.1k outlier both mis-raised the outer coefficient (getting B=+-A^4) and then divided one given condition by the other; the ratio produced a degree-9 equation in the center, and it burned roughly half its output trial-substituting integer centers before stumbling onto the branch. The revision therefore pins cancellation to the common factor AB only, and explicitly bans ratioing two conditions in favour of add-to-pin-the-center / subtract-to-pin-the-scale, both portable moves for any two-condition symmetric system.

hints.hint: To find how many repeats restore the original, trace; don't theorize. One repeat = ALL listed sub-steps in order, each acting on what the previous produced; the last sub-step alone is NOT the operation. Label slots distinctly and rewrite the whole state per sub-step: swapping two adjacent length-L blocks concatenates them in the other order, rest copied. That is L parallel slot-swaps, not one transposition, and nested sub-steps share slots, so never disjoint swaps: if your composite's cycles equal one sub-step's own cycles, you dropped the others. Reapply the whole repeat, writing each state, until it FIRST equals the original. If a permutation table gives a smaller order than your states, you wrote it inverted; rebuild from the states, don't argue. Cite no cycle length you did not trace. Do the two smallest sizes, fit ONE formula growing in the size, check one larger.
hints.subagent_summary: 2/8 with the incumbent. Three failures boxed 2 by writing confident cycle notation for the composite that is really just the LAST sub-step's swap (e.g. pairing each slot with the one a half-length shift away), i.e. earlier sub-steps silently vanished; the incumbent's nested-ranges clause did not catch it because they never traced a state at all. One capped-out rollout had a correct 4-repeat trace for the smallest nontrivial size, built a permutation table with the inverse convention, saw order 2, and burned its whole budget re-arguing which was right instead of trusting the states. Two more fabricated cycle lengths never traced (a 5-cycle plus 3-cycle; a 6-cycle for one size, an 8-cycle for the next) and fit growth laws to those invented numbers. So the revision names the drop-all-but-last-sub-step signature, makes the written trace override a contradicting table, and bans uncited cycle lengths.
